rv.q: It does feel like some of the storytelling moments haven’t fully coalesced into the production as a whole...But at its best, A History of Water has an intoxicating, headily persuasive energy to it.'
It is highly original in form, staged with great animation by Stef O’Driscoll in the Theatre Upstairs and full of impassioned concern.

It's a huge, troubling subject, given a witty, imaginative treatment. But the show feels rather packed and restless: so fearful of being boring that it whistles through material too fast for you to absorb it.
But the ingredients are not melded together: anecdote and didacticism fight each other.
But the finished piece is bitty, flimsy and, in places, hard to follow.
It's an interesting project that wears its politics on its sleeve, with moments that sparkle.
Not quite a lecture, not quite a play, Sabrina Mahfouz's meditation on power politics, feminism and her Egyptian-British heritage aims high, but ultimately resembles a promising first draft.

This is an evening of muddled, sandblasted polemic, decorated by maps of Middle East countries, bursts of free verse and a swirl of music that, though well drummed by Kareem Samara, is too loud. That makes it hard to hear Mahfouz and her co-performer Laura Hanna — a relief.
This journey may only take 70 minutes but it's an intense, mind-expanding way to spend the time.
And although the metaphor of water is a powerful one, I left the theatre only partially nourished: I wanted much more of everything.
A History of Water in the Middle East is a timely ingenious hybrid, worth taking in twice.
A History of Water is a raw, truthful, and exposed piece of theatre that tries to do a lot in just over an hour – but leaves me with goosebumps from start to finish.
Stef O’Driscoll’s inventive production will appeal to a young audience.

cn.t: Critics praise this passionate "gig-lecture" hybrid for its inventive blend of poetry, music, and anti-imperialist politics, though some find it overstuffed and more like a revision session than cohesive theater.
